title: FeatureMAP Tutorial
section: FeatureMAP: A Feature-based Metabolite Functional Module Identification and Annotation Pipeline
text:
FeatureMAP: A Feature-based Metabolite Functional Module Identification and Annotation Pipeline
FeatureMAP (featuremap) is a feature-centric framework for untargeted metabolomics that identifies biologically meaningful metabolic modules directly from metabolomic data, rather than relying only on predefined pathways or fully confirmed metabolite identities. It is developed by the Shen Lab at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore.
The package provides a five-step workflow:

Data preparation: prepare a valid feature table and optional MS2 annotation table for FeatureMAP.
Feature annotation: annotate raw LC-MS features to metabolite candidates using MS1 (and optional MS2) information.
Subnetwork extraction: construct a robust prize-collecting Steiner forest (PCSF)-based metabolic subnetwork.
Module identification: detect functional modules by community detection and evaluate module significance.
Module annotation: interpret significant modules with database knowledge, optional PubMed evidence, and optional LLM summarization.

This workflow helps convert feature-level metabolomics signals into interpretable biological modules in a reproducible and analysis-ready format.

title: FeatureMAP Tutorial
text:
Aim of This Tutorial
This guide walks you through the two faces of FeatureMAP: the R package for command-line (code-based) workflow and the Shiny App/Web version for point-and-click exploration. In the end, you will be able to:

Prepare a valid feature table for FeatureMAP.
Run the complete five-step FeatureMAP workflow with R code.
Complete the same analysis with the FeatureMAP Shiny App/Web interface.
Understand and inspect key result objects and module-level interpretations.

Whether you favour the command line or a browser, this tutorial gives you everything you need to apply FeatureMAP confidently in your metabolomics projects.

title: 2  Data Preparation
text:
2.1 Input Data Format Requirements
This chapter describes how to prepare input data for the FeatureMAP pipeline. Unlike traditional workflows, FeatureMAP starts from feature-level metabolomics data.

title: 2  Data Preparation
text:
2.1.1 Required feature_table
FeatureMAP requires a data frame named feature_table with the following columns:








Column
Type
Description




variable_id
character
Unique feature ID (no duplicates)


mz
numeric
Feature m/z


rt
numeric
Retention time


polarity
character
Ion mode, must be "positive" or "negative"


mean_intensity
numeric
Mean intensity of the feature


condition
numeric
Numeric value representing the direction and magnitude of association for each feature, such as a log fold change, regression coefficient, or correlation coefficient


pvalue
numeric
Statistical p-value corresponding to the association measure in condition, used to reflect the strength of evidence









Note



condition captures the effect direction and size, while pvalue reflects its statistical significance. Together, they are used downstream to prioritize features before PCSF subnetwork extraction.




2.1.2 Optional ms2_table
You can optionally provide an MS2 annotation table to improve feature-to-metabolite mapping confidence. MS2-based metabolite annotations can be obtained using the tidymass ecosystem.
Expected columns:

variable_id (character, unique)
HMDB.ID or KEGG.ID (character, can contain NA)

If ms2_table = NULL, FeatureMAP will proceed with MS1-based annotation only.

title: 2  Data Preparation
text:
2.3 Prepare Your Own Data
A typical preprocessing pattern is:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)

feature_table <- read_csv("your_feature_table.csv") %>%
  transmute(
    variable_id = as.character(variable_id),
    mz = as.numeric(mz),
    rt = as.numeric(rt),
    polarity = as.character(polarity),
    mean_intensity = as.numeric(mean_intensity),
    condition = as.numeric(condition),
    pvalue = as.numeric(pvalue)
  )

title: 2  Data Preparation
text:
2.4 Pre-run Checklist
Run these checks before Step 2:

required_cols <- c("variable_id", "mz", "rt", "polarity", "mean_intensity", "condition", "pvalue")
setdiff(required_cols, colnames(feature_table))
# should return character(0)

anyDuplicated(feature_table$variable_id)
# should return 0

all(feature_table$polarity %in% c("positive", "negative"))
# should return TRUE

sum(is.na(feature_table[, required_cols]))
# ideally 0 for required fields

title: 3  Feature Annotation
text:
3.1 What annotate_feature() Does
This chapter describes Step 2 of the FeatureMAP pipeline: feature-level metabolite annotation using annotate_feature().
annotate_feature() performs feature-to-metabolite candidate annotation for LC–MS data and resolves the many-to-many relationship between features and metabolites. The procedure consists of below main stages:
The function returns a featuremap_result object with stage marker "feature_annotated", which is required for all downstream analyses.

title: 3  Feature Annotation
text:
MS1 database matching: Each LC–MS feature is matched to metabolite databases (e.g., KEGG or HMDB) using accurate mass and common ion forms.
Metabolite Feature Cluster (MFC) construction: Features annotated to the same metabolite are grouped into MFCs based on retention-time proximity and ion relationships (e.g., adducts or isotopes).
Evidence-based scoring of MFCs: Each cluster is scored based on supporting evidence such as MS2 annotations, adduct types, and isotopic patterns.
Iterative refinement of annotations: Conflicting annotations are resolved iteratively by removing low-confidence clusters and ambiguous feature assignments until convergence.

title: 3  Feature Annotation
text:
3.4 Optional: Integrate MS2 Annotation
If you already have an MS2 annotation table, pass it to ms2_table:

ms2_table <- read.csv("your_ms2_annotation.csv")

res <- annotate_feature(
  feature_table = feature_table,
  ms2_table = ms2_table,
  refdata = "kegg"
)

Providing MS2 annotations is optional but can improve confidence in metabolite candidate assignments.

To understand how annotation ambiguity was reduced, inspect:

title: 3  Feature Annotation
text:
3.6 Next Step
Once feature annotation is complete, continue to Subnetwork Extraction to refine annotations with network context and extract the metabolic subnetwork.

title: 4  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
4.1 What extract_subnetwork() Does
This chapter describes Step 3 of the FeatureMAP pipeline: extracting a robust metabolic subnetwork with extract_subnetwork() using the prize-collecting Steiner forest (PCSF) strategy.
extract_subnetwork() integrates the refined feature annotations from Step 2 with a metabolic reaction network (MRN) and applies repeated PCSF optimization to identify a robust subnetwork.
At a high level, this step does the following:
This step moves the analysis from individual annotated features to a network-supported metabolite subnetwork, which is then used in downstream module extraction and interpretation.

title: 4  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
Compute feature importance: Feature-level statistical evidence is summarized from condition and pvalue and used to prioritize annotated metabolites.
Build feature–metabolite mappings: The refined annotation table is converted into feature–metabolite pairs that connect observed LC–MS features to candidate metabolites in the network.
Run repeated PCSF optimization: PCSF is run multiple times with random edge perturbation to reduce sensitivity to a single optimization result.
Aggregate robust network components: Node and edge frequencies are recorded across repeated runs, and the final subnetwork is constructed as the union of recurrent PCSF solutions.
Refine annotation using network support: Feature–metabolite mappings are updated based on network evidence, producing anno_feature_table2.

text:
4.2 Key Parameters








Parameter
Default
Description




res
required
featuremap_result returned by annotate_feature()


feature
"all"
Use all annotated features ("all") or only significant features ("sig")


pcutoff
0.05
Significance cutoff used when feature = "sig"


mrn
NULL
Optional custom metabolic reaction network (igraph); automatically loaded if NULL

100
Number of repeated PCSF runs


workers
4
Number of parallel workers


b
40
Prize scaling factor in PCSF


mu
1e-4
Hub penalty coefficient in PCSF


w
30
Dummy edge cost in PCSF


r
0.30
Magnitude of random edge perturbation across repeated runs


grid_tune
FALSE
Whether to tune b and w over a parameter grid


b_grid, w_grid

Candidate values of b and w when grid tuning is enabled


times_tune

Number of repeated runs for each (b, w) combination during tuning

title: 4  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
4.3 Basic Usage

# res is the output from Step 2 (annotate_feature)
res <- extract_subnetwork(
  res = res,
  feature = "sig",
  pcutoff = 0.05,
  mrn = NULL,
  workers = 4,
  times = 100,
  b = 40,
  mu = 1e-4,
  w = 30,
  r = 0.30,
  grid_tune = FALSE
)

title: 4  Subnetwork Extraction
section: 4.4 Optional: Grid Tuning for b and w
text:
4.4 Optional: Grid Tuning for b and w
If you want data-driven parameter selection, enable grid tuning:

res <- extract_subnetwork(
  res = res,
  feature = "sig",
  pcutoff = 0.05,
  workers = 4,
  times = 100,
  grid_tune = TRUE,
  b_grid = seq(20, 40, by = 5),
  w_grid = seq(25, 40, by = 5),
  times_tune = 10
)

When grid_tune = TRUE, FeatureMAP records:

res$tuning_grid: full tuning results
res$tuning_best: selected best (b, w) and summary metrics

title: 4  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
4.6 Next Step
Once subnetwork extraction is complete, continue to Module Identification to detect connected functional modules from the extracted network.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
5.1 What identify_module() Does
This chapter describes Step 4 of the FeatureMAP pipeline: identifying functional modules from the PCSF-derived subnetwork using identify_module().
identify_module() performs community detection on the extracted subnetwork and then evaluates module significance using permutation testing.
At a high level, this step performs the following operations:
This step converts the extracted metabolic network into functional modules supported by both network topology and feature-level statistical evidence.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
Construct a module detection graph: A metabolite-only subgraph is derived from the PCSF subnetwork. Steiner nodes with low occurrence frequency can be filtered using node_freq.
Detect network communities: Community detection algorithms are applied to partition the network into candidate modules.
Build module membership table: Node-to-module assignments are recorded in module_table.
Compute module activity scores: Module scores summarize the statistical signal from features mapped to metabolites within the module.
Assess statistical significance: A permutation procedure is used to estimate empirical significance and control false discovery rate.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
5.4 Clustering Methods

louvain
A fast modularity optimization algorithm that iteratively merges nodes and communities to maximize network modularity. It is widely used for large biological networks.
leading_eigen
A spectral method that partitions the network based on the leading eigenvectors of the modularity matrix. It identifies communities by separating nodes according to their contribution to modularity.
fast_greedy
An agglomerative hierarchical clustering method that starts with each node as its own community and progressively merges communities to increase modularity.
walktrap
A random-walk-based community detection algorithm that simulates short random walks on the network. The intuition is that random walks tend to remain within densely connected regions.

Different algorithms may produce slightly different module boundaries. Comparing multiple methods can help evaluate module robustness.

Hidden metabolites are not directly supported by measured features, but may provide important network context.

# 1      1         148             130    1.3944882 0.004536258 0.2177404
# 2     15          80              66    0.8717769 0.058164843 0.9960879
# 3     19          37              33    0.7624376 0.095688593 0.9960879
# 4     17          21              20    0.6974986 0.127492917 0.9960879
# 5     14          51              47    0.6885808 0.132541184 0.9960879
# 6      3          50              48    0.5985351 0.194456787 0.9960879

Important columns include:

Module – module identifier
Module_size – number of metabolite nodes in the module
Annotated_nodes – number of nodes supported by feature annotations
Module_score – aggregated activity score of the module
p – permutation-based p-value
fdr – multiple-testing corrected p-value

Modules with lower p or fdr values indicate stronger statistical support and are typically prioritized for downstream biological interpretation.






Tip



If too many tiny modules appear, increase min_size or tighten node_freq. If modules are too coarse, try alternative methods or relax these cutoffs.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
5.6 Next Step
Once modules are identified, continue to Function Annotation to interpret significant modules in biological terms.

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.1 What annotate_module() Does
This chapter describes Step 5 of the FeatureMAP pipeline: annotating statistically supported modules with annotate_module().
annotate_module() performs module-level biological interpretation for statistically supported modules in Step 4.
This step integrates three sources of information:
Only modules passing the significance cutoff (p or fdr) are annotated. This step converts statistically identified network modules into interpretable biological hypotheses.

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
Metabolite annotation summary: Metabolites contained in each significant module are summarized using the selected reference namespace (kegg or hmdb).
Optional literature retrieval: Relevant PubMed articles are retrieved and ranked for the top metabolites in each module.
LLM-based interpretation: A language model synthesizes module-level interpretations including title, summary, confidence label, and reasoning.

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.2 Key Parameters








Parameter
Default
Description




res
required
featuremap_result returned by identify_module()


p
"fdr"
Column in res$module_score used for filtering


pcutoff
0.05
Threshold applied to the selected significance column


ref_data
NULL
Optional functional reference annotation table


species
"human"
Species context used in module interpretation


biospecimen
NULL
Biospecimen context (e.g. plasma, serum, tissue)


phenotype
NULL
Disease or phenotype context


pubmed
TRUE
Whether to retrieve PubMed evidence


years
5
Time window for literature search


top_paper
3
Number of retained papers per metabolite


min_similarity
0.6
Embedding similarity cutoff used to filter literature


provider
"openai"
LLM and embedding provider. Currently supported options include "openai", "gemini", and "siliconflow"


embed_model
"text-embedding-3-small"
Embedding model used for literature ranking (model availability depends on the selected provider)


llm_model
"gpt-4.1-mini"
Language model used for module interpretation (model availability depends on the selected provider)


NCBI_api_key
""
NCBI Entrez API key for PubMed


llm_api_key
""
API key for the selected LLM provider









Note



If ref_data = NULL, FeatureMAP automatically loads the functional reference resource corresponding to the metabolite namespace used in earlier steps.








Tip



How to obtain an LLM API key
FeatureMAP currently supports "openai", "gemini", and "siliconflow" as LLM providers.
You can apply for an API key from the corresponding official platform:

OpenAI: https://platform.openai.com/
Gemini (Google AI Studio): https://ai.google.dev/aistudio
SiliconFlow: https://siliconflow.cn/









Tip



How to obtain a PubMed / NCBI API key
If you enable PubMed retrieval, you need to apply for an NCBI API key for higher request limits: https://account.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/settings/

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.3 Basic Usage

Database + LLM onlyDatabase + PubMed + LLM



res <- annotate_module(
  res = res,
  p = "fdr",
  pcutoff = 0.05,
  ref_data = NULL,
  species = "human",
  biospecimen = "plasma",
  phenotype = "disease phenotype",
  pubmed = FALSE,
  provider = "openai",
  llm_model = "gpt-4.1-mini",
  llm_api_key = "your llm api key"
)




res <- annotate_module(
  res = res,
  p = "fdr",
  pcutoff = 0.05,
  ref_data = NULL,
  species = "human",
  biospecimen = "plasma",
  phenotype = "disease phenotype",
  pubmed = TRUE,
  years = 5,
  top_paper = 3,
  min_similarity = 0.6,
  provider = "openai",
  embed_model = "text-embedding-3-small",
  llm_model = "gpt-4.1-mini",
  NCBI_api_key = "your ncbi api key",
  llm_api_key = "your llm api key"
)










Note




Provide species, biospecimen, and phenotype whenever possible
Use API keys from environment variables rather than hard-coding them

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.4 Result Interpretation
After successful annotation:

res$stage
# [1] "module_annotated"

res$module_function$title
# [1] "Nucleotide Metabolism and Cofactor-Linked Energy Transfer"

res$module_function$summary
# [1] "This module primarily represents biochemical processes centered on 
# nucleotide metabolism, including purine nucleotide synthesis and turnover, 
# as indicated by the high importance and robustness of purine nucleotides such 
# as phosphoribosyl-ATP, ADP, and ATP. The presence of ribose phosphate derivatives 
# and organooxygen compounds supports active ribose phosphate metabolism, which 
# is essential for nucleotide biosynthesis. Additionally, the module includes 
# pyridines and derivatives like pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate, highlighting involvement 
# in coenzyme-dependent amino acid metabolism and transamination reactions. The 
# medium structural stability and low signal concentration suggest a coordinated 
# pathway-level shift rather than a hub-driven signal. Fatty acyls with high 
# importance also suggest ancillary roles in acyl-CoA metabolism linked to energy 
# homeostasis. The presence of tetrapyrroles and molybdenum cofactors further 
# indicates involvement in redox and enzymatic cofactor functions. Overall, this 
# module reflects integrated nucleotide biosynthesis and cofactor-mediated metabolic 
# energy processes."

res$module_function$confidence_label
# [1] "high"

res$module_function$rationale
# [1] "The inferred function is biologically plausible in humans and detectable 
# in plasma, where nucleotide metabolites and cofactors circulate. These pathways 
# are relevant to systemic metabolic regulation and could be linked to age-related 
# metabolic changes, supporting high confidence."

head(res$module_top_metabolite_pmids %>% 
       arrange(PMID_rank))
#   Module Module_label Compound_ID                                    Compound_name PMID_rank     PMID
# 1      1      module1      C20978                                    Glucoselysine         1 38879006
# 2      1      module1      C00647                           Pyridoxamine phosphate         1 38846080
# 3      1      module1      C02739                      1-(5-Phospho-D-ribosyl)-ATP        NA     <NA>
# 4      1      module1      C11039 2'-Deoxy-5-hydroxymethylcytidine-5'-triphosphate        NA     <NA>
# 5      1      module1      C01244               3,5-Diiodo-4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate        NA     <NA>
# 6      1      module1      C15761                                   Concanamycin A        NA     <NA>
#                                                                                                                                             title
# 1 Glucoselysine, a unique advanced glycation end-product of the polyol pathway and its association with vascular complications in type 2 diabetes.
# 2                 Why pyridoxal phosphate could be a functional predecessor of thiamine pyrophosphate and speculations on a primordial metabolism.
# 3                                                                                                                                             <NA>
# 4                                                                                                                                             <NA>
# 5                                                                                                                                             <NA>
# 6                                                                                                                                             <NA>
#   score_embed
# 1   0.6432722
# 2   0.6080499
# 3          NA
# 4          NA
# 5          NA
# 6          NA


6.4.1 Module interpretation table
module_function contains the final module-level interpretation generated by the LLM. Important fields include:

module_id – the module ID identified by previous step
title – a concise functional label summarizing the dominant biological theme of the module
summary – a paragraph-level interpretation of the module based on metabolite composition, network context, and optional literature evidence
confidence_label – a qualitative confidence level for the interpretation
rationale – a short explanation of why the inferred function is biologically plausible in the specified study context
raw_response – the original LLM response retained for transparency

This table provides a concise interpretation of each statistically supported module.


6.4.2 Literature evidence table
When pubmed = TRUE, FeatureMAP also returns ranked PubMed evidence (module_top_metabolite_pmids) for top metabolites in each module.

Module and Module_label – the module being annotated
Compound_ID and Compound_name – the metabolite used for literature retrieval
PMID_rank – the rank of the selected paper for that metabolite
PMID – PubMed identifier
title – article title
score_embed – semantic relevance score used for literature ranking

Higher score_embed values indicate stronger semantic relevance between the literature and the module context.

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.5 Common Issues

PubMed retrieval is slow Start with fewer modules, a shorter years window, or pubmed = FALSE for validation.
No useful literature retained Relax min_similarity, increase years, or provide a more specific phenotype.
Provider/model mismatch Make sure the selected provider, embed_model, and llm_model are compatible.

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.6 Practical Checks Before Running

head(res$module_score)
sum(res$module_score$fdr < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

If this count is zero, it is better to revisit Step 4 before trying module annotation.

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.7 Next Step
Module annotation is the last step of the current R-package tutorial workflow. If needed, you can next inspect res$module_function and the PubMed evidence tables for downstream reporting or visualization.
If you want to continue with the interactive interface, move to Shiny App Installation to start the Shiny tutorial.

title: 7  Installation
7  Installation
text:
Tip



How to Launch the Shiny App

In an R session, run: featuremapshiny::run_featuremap()
An R viewer window will open where you can start the workflow. You can also use the Open in Browser button to launch it in your default web browser.
You can stop the app at any time by closing the browser tab/window or pressing the stop button in your R IDE.

title: 7  Installation
text:
7.2 Web Access
A hosted, browser-based instance of FeatureMAP Shiny is planned for users who prefer not to manage a local R environment. The service will provide the same point-and-click interface as the local Shiny application and will require no installation.
Planned Access URL: https://www.shen-lab.org/featuremap_shiny






Note



The workflow described in the following Shiny chapters applies to both the local featuremapshiny package and the future hosted web deployment.


Once you install the FeatureMAP shiny successfully, continue to next step.

title: 8  Data Preparation
text:
8.1 Start From Home Page
This chapter focuses on how to use the first part of FeatureMAP Shiny rather than repeating all data-format details from the R package tutorial. If you need the full input specification, please refer to R package-Data Preparation, especially Section 2.1.
Launch the app with:
featuremapshiny::run_featuremap()
When the app opens, you will first see the Home page. In the center of the page, there are two main buttons:
Here we click the button Get Started to start the analysis pipeline.

title: 8  Data Preparation
text:
Get Started: jump directly to Data Upload, which is the first analysis step
Documentation: open the FeatureMAP Shiny documentation repository in your browser

title: 8  Data Preparation
text:
8.2 Data Upload Page
Data Upload is Step 1 of the workflow. This page is mainly divided into two areas:

Parameter area on the left: choose the reference database, upload files, and click Load
Result area on the right: preview the loaded feature table and check the loading status

title: 8  Data Preparation
text:
8.3 What You Need to Provide
Compared with the R package tutorial, the main points to remember here are:

a feature table is required
an MS2 annotation table is optional
you need to choose either HMDB or KEGG as the reference database
you can use either the built-in reference data or upload your own reference datasets

The current Shiny app accepts uploaded data tables in:.csv, .rda, and .RData.
For detailed column definitions of feature_table and ms2_table, see R package-Data Preparation.

title: 8  Data Preparation
text:
8.4 Recommended: Start with Demo Data
For most users, the best way to learn the app is to start with the built-in demo data.
The recommended sequence is:

choose HMDB or KEGG
click Use Demo Data
keep Default reference (recommended) unless you specifically want to test custom references
click Load
confirm that the preview table and status message appear on the right






This lets you move through the full Shiny workflow first, before switching to your own dataset.






Tip



After clicking Use Demo Data, the app only stages the demo files. You still need to click Load to actually place them into the current session.

title: 8  Data Preparation
text:
8.5 Next Step
Once the data are loaded successfully, click Next Step to continue to Feature Annotation.

title: 9  Feature Annotation
text:
9.1 Enter the Feature Annotation Page
This chapter focuses on how to use Step 2: Feature Annotation in FeatureMAP Shiny. The detailed method, parameter definitions, and output structure have already been introduced in R package-Feature Annotation, so here we focus on the app workflow itself.
After finishing Data Upload, click Next Step or select Feature Annotation from the top navigation bar.
This page is also divided into two areas:
The purpose of this step is to map metabolomics features to candidate metabolites and prepare the refined annotation table for downstream network analysis.

title: 9  Feature Annotation
text:
Parameter area on the left: set annotation parameters and click Run
Result area on the right: view the annotation summary and detailed result table

title: 9  Feature Annotation
text:
9.2 Parameter Area
The left panel is where you set the feature annotation parameters before clicking Run. Since the detailed meanings of these parameters have already been introduced in R package-Feature Annotation, we do not repeat them here.






Note



If you are running the demo data for the first time, it is usually best to keep the default settings and run the step once before tuning anything.

title: 9  Feature Annotation
text:
9.3 Run Feature Annotation
Once the parameters are ready, click Run.
The app will start the feature annotation procedure and show a running-status modal. When the step finishes successfully, the result panel on the right will be updated automatically, and the Next Step button will become available.
If you did not provide an MS2 annotation table in the previous step, the app will still run using MS1-based annotation only.

title: 9  Feature Annotation
text:
9.4 Result Area

9.4.1 Summary
The Summary tab gives a quick overview of the annotation results. It mainly helps you see how the annotation changed before and after refinement at both the metabolite level and the feature level.





This view is useful for checking whether the annotation step completed normally and whether the refinement reduced redundancy.


9.4.2 Annotation Table 1
The Annotation Table 1 tab contains the detailed feature-to-metabolite annotation results produced by this step.





For a full explanation of the result columns, see R package-3 Feature Annotation.
Below the table, the app also shows an Annotation Status summary, including:

how many features were annotated
how many feature-metabolite entries were produced
the average number of metabolite candidates per annotated feature

title: 9  Feature Annotation
section: 9.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
text:
9.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
If you followed the previous chapter and loaded the built-in demo data, the recommended workflow here is:

keep the default parameter settings
click Run
wait for the annotation step to finish
check the Summary tab first
then open Annotation Table 1 to inspect the detailed annotation results

This is the easiest way to understand what the step produces before applying it to your own dataset.






Tip



If the result table looks empty, first check whether Data Upload finished successfully in the previous step, and then confirm that the selected reference database and input files were loaded correctly.

title: 9  Feature Annotation
text:
9.6 Next Step
Once feature annotation is complete, click Next Step to continue to Subnetwork Extraction.

title: 10  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
10.1 Enter the PCSF Subnetwork Page
This chapter focuses on how to use Step 3: Subnetwork Extraction in FeatureMAP Shiny. The detailed method, parameter definitions, and result structure have already been introduced in R package-Subnetwork Extraction, so here we focus on the Shiny workflow itself.
After finishing Feature Annotation, click Next Step or select PCSF Subnetwork from the navigation bar. This page is also divided into two areas:
The purpose of this step is to use the PCSF strategy to extract a network-supported metabolite subnetwork for downstream module identification.

title: 10  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
Parameter area on the left: set the subnetwork extraction options and click Run PCSF
Result area on the right: inspect the extracted subnetwork and the refined annotation results

title: 10  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
10.2 Parameter Area
The left panel is where you set the PCSF-related parameters before clicking Run PCSF. Since the detailed meanings of these parameters have already been introduced in R package-Subnetwork Extraction, we do not repeat them here.






Note



If you are running the demo data for the first time, it is usually best to keep the default settings, leave grid tuning off, and run the step once before changing anything.

title: 10  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
10.3 Run PCSF Subnetwork Extraction
Once the parameters are ready, click Run PCSF.
The app will start the PCSF subnetwork extraction procedure and show a running-status modal. When the step finishes successfully, the result panel on the right will be updated automatically, and the Next Step button will become available.
If you enable grid tuning, the app will additionally report the selected best parameter combination after the run finishes.

title: 10  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
10.4 Result Area

10.4.1 Subnetwork
The Subnetwork tab is used to inspect the extracted PCSF network. If Visualize PCSF subnetwork is enabled in the parameter area, this tab will show the network plot directly in the app. If visualization is disabled, the run can still finish normally, but the plot area will remain empty.











Tip



This network plot is interactive in the Shiny app. You can zoom, drag, and click nodes to explore the subnetwork in more detail.


When grid tuning is enabled, the best selected parameter combination is also shown in this tab after the analysis is complete.


10.4.2 Annotation Table 2
The Annotation Table 2 tab contains the network-refined annotation results generated after PCSF extraction. Compared with the previous annotation table, this table reflects the additional support from the extracted subnetwork and is the main output that will be carried into the next step.





For a full explanation of the result columns, see R package-Subnetwork Extraction.
Below the table, the app also shows an Annotation Status summary, including:

how many features were matched in the refined table
how many feature-metabolite entries were retained
the average number of entries per matched feature

title: 10  Subnetwork Extraction
section: 10.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
text:
10.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
If you followed the previous chapters and loaded the built-in demo data, the recommended workflow here is:

keep the default parameter settings
leave Enable grid tuning unchecked for the first run
optionally enable Visualize PCSF subnetwork if you want to see the network directly
click Run PCSF
check the Subnetwork tab first
then open Annotation Table 2 to inspect the refined results

This is the easiest way to understand what the PCSF step produces before tuning parameters on your own dataset.






Tip



If the result tab stays empty, first check whether Feature Annotation finished successfully in the previous step.

title: 10  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
10.6 Next Step
Once subnetwork extraction is complete, click Next Step to continue to Module Identification.

title: 11  Module Identification
text:
11.1 Enter the Module Identification Page
This chapter focuses on how to use Step 4: Module Identification in FeatureMAP Shiny. The detailed method, parameter definitions, and result structure have already been introduced in R package-Module Identification, so here we focus on the Shiny workflow itself.
After finishing Subnetwork Extraction, click Next Step or select Module Identification from the top navigation bar. This page is also divided into two areas:
The purpose of this step is to identify functional modules from the extracted PCSF subnetwork.

title: 11  Module Identification
text:
Parameter area on the left: set the module identification options and click Run
Result area on the right: inspect the detected modules from different views

title: 11  Module Identification
text:
11.2 Parameter Area
The left panel is where you set the module identification parameters before clicking Run. Since the detailed meanings of these parameters have already been introduced in R package-Module Identification, we do not repeat them here.






Note



If you are running the demo data for the first time, it is usually best to keep the default settings and run the step once before tuning the algorithm or filtering thresholds.

title: 11  Module Identification
text:
11.3 Run Module Identification
Once the parameters are ready, click Run.
The app will start module identification and show a running-status modal. When the step finishes successfully, the result panel on the right will be updated automatically, and the Next Step button will become available.

title: 11  Module Identification
text:
11.4 Result Area

11.4.1 Visualization
The Visualization tab is used to inspect the detected modules as subnetworks.





After the run finishes, you can choose a module and view its network directly in the app. This is usually the most intuitive place to start, because it lets you quickly see how the selected module is organized.


11.4.2 Module Score
The Module Score tab shows the quantitative summary for identified modules. This table is useful for checking which modules are stronger or more statistically convincing before moving on to interpretation.





For a full explanation of the score-related columns, see R package-Module Identification.


11.4.3 Module Table
The Module Table tab shows the detailed module membership results. This table is the main reference when you want to inspect which metabolites were assigned to each module and what information will be passed to the next step.





For a full explanation of the result columns, see R package-Module Identification.

title: 11  Module Identification
section: 11.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
text:
11.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
If you followed the previous chapters and loaded the built-in demo data, the recommended workflow here is:

keep the default parameter settings
click Run
wait for module identification to finish
open Visualization first to inspect the detected modules
then review Module Score
finally check Module Table for the detailed module membership results

This is the easiest way to understand what this step produces before tuning parameters on your own dataset.






Tip



If no module appears, first check whether Subnetwork Extraction finished successfully in the previous step and whether the extracted subnetwork contains enough structure for module detection.

title: 11  Module Identification
text:
11.6 Next Step
Once module identification is complete, click Next Step to continue to AI-Powered Function Annotation.

title: 12  Function Annotation
text:
12.1 Enter the Function Annotation Page
This chapter focuses on how to use Step 5: AI-Powered Function Annotation in FeatureMAP Shiny. The detailed method, parameter definitions, and result structure have already been introduced in R package-Function Annotation, so here we focus on the Shiny workflow itself.
After finishing Module Identification, click Next Step or select Function Annotation from the top navigation bar. This page is also divided into two areas:
The purpose of this step is to generate interpretable biological summaries for significant modules using database knowledge, optional PubMed evidence, and a large language model.

title: 12  Function Annotation
text:
Parameter area on the left: set the module filtering and annotation options, then click Run
Result area on the right: inspect the module-level biological interpretation results

title: 12  Function Annotation
text:
12.2 Parameter Area
The left panel is where you set the function annotation parameters before clicking Run. Since the detailed meanings of these parameters have already been introduced in R package-Function Annotation, we do not repeat them here.
The main point to remember is:

you can run this step with database information plus LLM interpretation
you can optionally enable PubMed literature for additional evidence
you must provide a valid LLM API key
if PubMed is enabled, you should also provide an NCBI API key







Note



If you are running the demo data for the first time, it is usually best to start with a simple configuration first, then enable PubMed-based annotation later if needed.

title: 12  Function Annotation
text:
12.3 Run Function Annotation
Once the parameters are ready, click Run.
The app will start module function annotation and show a running-status modal. When the step finishes successfully, the result panel on the right will be updated automatically.
If no significant modules pass the selected cutoff, the app will finish normally but return an empty result for this step.

title: 12  Function Annotation
text:
12.4 Result Area
After the run finishes, the right panel shows the annotation result for one selected module at a time.





If literature-based annotation was enabled, the page also shows a Literature Evidence (PMID) section for the selected module. This section helps you inspect which literature evidence was retained and gives you a quick way to open the corresponding PubMed records.

title: 12  Function Annotation
section: 12.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
text:
12.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
If you followed the previous chapters and loaded the built-in demo data, the recommended workflow here is:

keep the default significance settings
start with the default reference database
provide the required LLM settings and API key
leave Use PubMed literature off for the first test run if you want a simpler setup
click Run
review the generated title, summary, confidence, and rationale for each module

This is the easiest way to understand what this step produces before running a more complete literature-supported annotation on your own dataset.






Tip



If this step returns no results, first check whether any significant modules were detected in Module Identification under your current cutoff.

title: 12  Function Annotation
text:
12.6 Next Step
Once function annotation is complete, go to Results to download the generated tables and networks.

title: 13  Results Export
text:
13.1 Enter the Results Page
This chapter focuses on how to use Step 6: Results in FeatureMAP Shiny. This page is the final export center of the Shiny workflow, where you can review the overall run summary, choose which outputs to export, and download them as a compressed package.
After finishing AI-Powered Function Annotation, click Go to Results or select Results from the top navigation bar.

title: 13  Results Export
text:
13.2 Summary Cards
At the top of the page, a row of small summary cards gives a quick overview of the current run. These cards summarize key information such as:

how many features were uploaded
how many features were retained in the refined annotation results
how many modules were detected
how many tables are currently export-ready

This section is useful for quickly checking whether the full workflow has run as expected before exporting anything.

title: 13  Results Export
text:
13.3 Export Options
The left panel is where you choose what to export.Here you can:

select which result tables to include
choose the table export format
choose whether to export network outputs
choose the network export format

The app packages the selected outputs into a single compressed archive for download.

title: 13  Results Export
text:
13.4 Selected Content Preview
Inside the Export Options panel, the app also shows a Selected Content preview.





This preview helps you confirm:

what you selected
whether each item is ready
whether anything is still unavailable because an earlier step has not finished yet

Only items that are ready can be successfully downloaded.

title: 13  Results Export
text:
13.5 Analysis Parameters
The right panel contains an Analysis Parameters card that summarizes key settings used in the current run. This panel provides a compact record of major settings from:





This is helpful when you want to double-check what settings were used before exporting results or preparing a report.

title: 13  Results Export
text:
13.6 Back to Home
The Back to Home button returns the app to the Home page after confirmation.





Before returning, the app clears the current analysis results stored in the running session, so you can start a new analysis from a clean state.






Note



This action clears the current in-app analysis state. It does not delete files that you have already downloaded to your own computer.

title: 13  Results Export
text:
13.7 Recommended Export Workflow
For most users, the recommended workflow on this page is:

check the summary cards at the top
choose the result tables you want to keep
choose the export format
optionally include network outputs
confirm readiness in Selected Content
click Download Results
click Back to Home

This gives you a clean backup of the current run in one compressed file.
